Barkoskie said his team found that Bardisa had attended college with the other nurse, who was also employed by AdventHealth but at a different hospital.

AdventHealth said that it could not comment on personnel issues or legal matters but that it was cooperating with the Flagler County Sheriff’s Office. “Patient safety is our highest priority,” it said in an emailed statement. “The license verification process across our system has become more automated and hardwired with the Department of Health in a way that minimizes human intervention.”

Bardisa’s attorney, Josh Davis, did not respond to a request for comment.

Nurse shortages, underfunding

Having some health care experience can allow impostors to avoid detection for longer, Mensik Kennedy said. Others might just bounce among facilities to avoid scrutiny.

State Trooper Anthony Sayles Jr., who led the investigation in Pennsylvania, said Womack was not licensed as a medical professional in the state and is not believed to have been licensed in any other state. Sayles found that Womack worked shifts in nine health care facilities in Pennsylvania starting in 2023 and that all of them subsequently placed her on their do-not-retain lists for misconduct.

“She just didn’t know basic knowledge,” Sayles said in an interview. “Every time that somebody was onto her, she would just pick up and go do her thing somewhere else.”

During the investigation, Sayles discovered that Womack was on Georgia’s impostor list and was wanted in New Jersey, Georgia and Tennessee, with warrants pending in other states. She is suspected of impersonating four nurses and using their identities to secure short-term jobs, authorities said.

Mensik Kennedy said these and other recent cases point to the need for health care facilities to do more stringent vetting. But she also said structural factors may make enforcement difficult. For one, state nursing boards, which are typically in charge of handing out licenses and investigating complaints, tend to be understaffed and underfunded, leading to delays and bottlenecks. By the time a state nursing board completes its investigation of a suspected fraudulent nurse, that person may have had time to flee to another state and obtain work there.

This situation was further complicated by the pandemic, Mensik Kennedy said, because some states relaxed licensing rules in an effort to get nurses licensed “as quick as possible.”

“There’s a lot of push, of course. We are in a nursing shortage. But we also need to make sure we do the process correctly and we have the staff to do that process correctly,” she said.

Operation Nightingale

In 2019, federal agents were tipped off that a Florida school was offering fraudulent nursing diplomas and transcripts. For up to $17,000, one could obtain the proof of education required to sit for the NCLEX, the nursing licensure exam, without having to take classes or do clinical work.

That sparked a years-long investigation, dubbed Operation Nightingale, after English nurse Florence Nightingale. Federal authorities said more than 7,600 fake diplomas were distributed by three Florida nursing schools, which are now closed, between 2016 and 2021. These schools had operated legitimately but were shut down because their students’ passing rate for the NCLEX was too low, said Fernando Porras, an assistant special agent in charge with the Miami regional office of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG).

“Coming off of covid, there was a significant opportunity for health care professionals to make more money,” Porras said. “Those that were unlicensed — they were maybe an aide at the hospital or a certified nursing assistant — realized that if they get better credentials and licensing, they could get higher pay and more opportunities.”

In total, 31 recruiters and school officials have been convicted in connection with Operation Nightingale, Porras said. States are still investigating some of those licenses. Of the more than 7,600 people who received fraudulent diplomas, about 2,100 passed the NCLEX, he said, and some had to take the test multiple times.

Porras said HHS-OIG did not identify any complaints relating to serious injuries or deaths of patients treated by nurses who obtained fraudulent diplomas and transcripts. He argued this is a sign that the safeguards built into the system actually worked, and says some nurses who obtained fraudulent diplomas may not have obtained or held onto jobs because they were not qualified.

Since Operation Nightingale, some health care facilities and state nursing boards have set new guardrails to prevent such large-scale diploma fraud, Porras said. Still, he said, nursing bodies and health care institutions must remain vigilant to protect the public: “One individual posing as a nurse with fake credentials is one nurse too many.”
item.author: Annabelle Timsit

item.title: He designed the Cracker Barrel logo. Now it’s caught in a culture war.
item.description:
Bill Holley would be thrilled the company kept his logo, his wife said: “I think Bill’s holding his hand up and saying, ‘I made Cracker Barrel great again!’”

Beverly Holley misses a lot of things about her husband of 59 years, but one is a specific little smile he’d crack.

It would happen on road trips through the South when the family would come across a Cracker Barrel sign. The couple’s two daughters would cry out, “Oh, Dad, there’s your logo!” Holley said her husband was humble, but he would let slip a small grin.

Bill Holley, who died in 2021, designed that Cracker Barrel logo — now the focal point of a culture war playing out among people on social media, members of Congress, a governor, one of Cracker Barrel’s competitors and President Donald Trump.

It started when the Tennessee-based restaurant chain, which has about 660 locations nationwide, unveiled a minimalist new logo last week that bore little resemblance to Holley’s original from 1977.

Other famous brands to which customers have strong emotional connections, such as Chuck E. Cheese, have faced backlash when they modernized to appeal to changing tastes. But this was something else. The redesign set off a firestorm, mainly from conservatives, who called the new design “woke,” causing the company’s stock to tumble.

Then Trump took up the cause of protecting the original logo.

“Make Cracker Barrel a WINNER again,” he wrote Tuesday on social media.

Hours later, the company reverted to Bill Holley’s logo, telling customers “we could’ve done a better job” and promising to “never change” its values.

Bill Holley would have been “thrilled” with the decision to keep his original logo, Beverly Holley told The Washington Post on Wednesday, less than 24 hours after the reversal.

“He would not have liked the plain Jane logo,” she said. “Because it really says nothing about the restaurant.”

Beverly Holley, 80, said her husband would have been pleased to see people — including those at the highest levels of government — rallying around his design.

“I think Bill’s holding his hand up and saying, ‘I made Cracker Barrel great again!’” she said.

Debbie Holley, one of the couple’s daughters, said her family “thought the sun rose and set in my dad,” so she was overjoyed to see his design restored.

“I was really happy that bit of highway culture was being saved,” she said.

Bill Holley’s version of the logo was born on a napkin during a meeting with Cracker Barrel founder Dan Evins, Beverly Holley said. The sketch depicted Evins’s Uncle Herschel sitting on a wooden chair and leaning on a barrel, and the words “Old Country Store” — all of which were eliminated in the briefly proposed redesign.

“I kept it for many, many years, and then [one day] I thought, we probably don’t need this,” Beverly Holley said of the napkin sketch. “I should have kept it — would be worth a lot today.”

She bemoaned incorrect memes spreading in recent days, including one asserting that Bill Holley’s work alluded to a slaveholder’s whip. The swooping line in the logo is actually a calligraphy flourish, according to PolitiFact. And the name refers to barrels of soda crackers that country stores used to sell.

Holley said her late husband designed for other large brands — including Red Lobster, Shoney’s and Lowe’s — but was most proud of the Cracker Barrel logo because it represented where he came from. He was born to a sharecropping family on a farm outside Petersburg, Tennessee, she said. He later moved to Nashville, his wife’s hometown, to attend design school.

She said she still remembers the two-tone green 1955 Pontiac that he drove when they met. He looked like a “young Robert Redford,” Beverly Holley said, and she wanted him to notice her.

He did. After he moved into the community where his future wife had grown up, he asked a young boy whether he knew her name and offered the kid a quarter. The boy said it would cost him 50 cents.

“Best investment he ever made,” Beverly Holley said with a laugh.

Although Bill Holley worked as an ad designer at the Nashville-based Buntin Group for nearly a half-century, Cracker Barrel was one of his first freelance clients.

Whenever the couple ate at a Cracker Barrel, she would tell the server: “Excuse me, do you know who this gentleman is? He designed your logo.”

Usually, she said, the server’s eyes would grow big and her husband would wave her off with an “Oh, Bev!” (He loved the restaurant’s white sausage gravy.)

The Buntin Group now offers a design scholarship in Bill Holley’s name. And a plaque bolted to the door of his former office there reads: “May all who take this office continue the legacy of selflessness, good cheer, talent and unending optimism represented by William ‘Bill’ Holley.”
item.author: Ben Brasch

item.title: Children prayed for ‘a future filled with hope.’ Then the gunfire began.
item.description:
On the southwest side of Minneapolis, a school shooter killed two students and injured more than a dozen others while classes celebrated their first Mass.

MINNEAPOLIS — The children filed into the pews of Annunciation Catholic Church on Wednesday morning for their first Mass of the new school year, a time of nervous energy and excitement. The theme of the coming term was borrowed from the prophet Jeremiah: “A future filled with hope.”

But just minutes into the service, as the students were reciting Psalm 139 — a call-and-answer prayer about God’s all-knowing love — the sound of gunfire ripped through the air and the church windows shattered. In an instant, the back-to-school glee dissolved into terror and chaos.

An assailant — later identified as 23-year-old Robin Westman — had stood outside the stately brown brick church on this city’s southwest side and aimed a rifle through the glass at the young worshipers within, authorities said. The shooter killed two children, ages 8 and 10, and injured 14 more before dying of a self-inflicted gunshot wound in the parking lot. Three elderly parishioners also were wounded.

The attack took place steps away from the church’s affiliated school, which enrolls students from preschool through eighth grade. It was the nation’s first school shooting since the end of summer break, expanding the list of communities to suffer from a uniquely American epidemic just three days into Annunciation’s fall semester.

Parents, priests and local leaders struggled to articulate the anguish they felt from such violence piercing a place they held sacred — a place that, as a school and a church, they saw as a refuge.

“There’s nothing about today that can fill us with hope,” said the school’s new principal, Matthew DeBoer, invoking the words of Jeremiah.

For Minneapolis, the pain echoed the trauma felt only two months ago when a gunman targeted two state lawmakers in their homes, killing Rep. Melissa Hortman and her husband, and injuring a colleague and his wife.

Speaking at a vigil in Lynnhurst Park on Wednesday evening, Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey said teachers and faculty at Annunciation “threw their bodies on top of children” to protect them as shots were being fired.

“They did the right thing to protect what could have been so many more children dead,” Frey said.

“But what we know is that far too often, people are robbed of that childhood because of this senseless gun violence,” he said. “And don’t let anybody tell you that it’s not about guns, because it is.”

Wednesday’s shooting began about 8:30 a.m. local time, police said, after Westman approached the house of worship armed with the rifle, plus a shotgun and a pistol. Within seconds, as bullets sprayed, teachers ducked their students beneath the sanctuary’s wooden pews, shielding them from fire.

“Our teachers were heroes,” DeBoer said at an afternoon news conference.

Students, too, scrambled to protect their classmates, he said. One fifth-grader watched his friend get shot in the back. Two other middle-schoolers had blood on their clothes when their mother picked them up. Children and at least one adult with a range of injuries were taken to three hospitals, some in critical condition. Several underwent surgery into the afternoon, officials said, but all were expected to live.

“The sheer cruelty and cowardice of firing into a church full of children is absolutely incomprehensible,” Minneapolis Police Chief Brian O’Hara said as church bells tolled behind him. While the pandemonium unfolded in the church, preschoolers attending class in a room below the sanctuary took cover — even hiding in a play kitchen there. Four-year-old Ayla told her father, Brooks Turner, that it sounded like “somebody was trying to break down the ceiling above them.” She heard a series of loud bangs.

Ayla and the other children lay down flat, and she covered her eyes. She didn’t want to see anything scary, Turner recounted. When they were finally evacuated, a police officer picked her up and carried her out. Ayla’s birthday made her just young enough to be placed in preschool, her father said. If she had been in kindergarten, she would have been upstairs celebrating Mass.

“It’s unimaginable what the parents are going through,” Turner said.

Vincent Francoual got a text from his wife about an active shooter at Annunciation shortly after dropping off their 11-year-old, Chloe.

“I was incredulous,” he said. “I didn’t really realize what was going on.”

He sped back to the neighborhood and found Chloe safe in the school gym. But she was inconsolable.

“We just cried and asked, ‘Are you okay?’” he said. His daughter described bleeding classmates and other kids sprawled on the floor. She had run to the church basement and pushed a table against the door, she told him.

Sixth-graders like Chloe are assigned second-grade buddies, and Francoual said his daughter has been racked with guilt because she wasn’t able to take her buddy with her. The younger child was later found unharmed.

“When your daughter tells you that she really thought she was going to die … I don’t know what to say to that,” Francoual said. “We’re trying to put the pieces together right now.”

Howard Dotson, a chaplain in Minneapolis, rushed to the area to help after seeing an “armada” of police cars racing there.

He waited with a parent at the perimeter that law enforcement had set up around the school, then went to a hall where families were being reunited with their children. Kids appeared to be in shock. Mothers were crying.

A teacher told him that students had sung “Lord Prepare Me To Be a Sanctuary” as they made their way from the chapel.

In the immediate aftermath, law enforcement swarmed the area, cordoning it off with yellow tape and blocking roads with vehicles. A drone flew overhead and FBI agents knocked on the doors of nearby homes.

A block from the church, Carla Maldonado broke into tears as she hugged another woman. Her young son and daughter stood beside her in their school uniforms — safe but still terrified.

Maldonado lives in the quiet neighborhood around Annunciation and heard the shooting begin. She rushed to the scene on foot. For her children, the horrific moments in church had been a blur. They remembered a barrage of gunfire, but they weren’t sure how many shots.

Laura Kirstein, who also lives nearby, watched in horror as parents ran toward the school to look for their children. She walked across the street to a neighbor, and they hugged and cried for several minutes. “We didn’t let go,” she said.

The Annunciation community is small and close-knit, members and neighbors said. Margaret Richards, whose children had attended the school years earlier, said its size and atmosphere draws many families.

“I’m sick to my stomach,” she said. “I can’t believe this is happening.”

By late afternoon, several vigils had been planned for that evening, a sign of how far and fast grief over the shooting had spread. Alberto Gurrieri, a pastor at an evangelical church in neighboring St. Paul, drove to Annunciation as soon as he heard the news, looking for someone to pray with.

“It breaks your heart,” he said. “You’re talking about children, talking about their first week of school, and we’re talking about the effects of sin and death in this world.”

“It makes you cry out to the Lord.”

Local authorities said they were still investigating the shooter’s motive, while the police chief referred to a “manifesto” that had circulated online but had since been removed. FBI Director Kash Patel said his agency is looking into whether the shooting constituted an act of domestic terrorism and a hate crime targeting Catholics.

Officials were working to learn more about Westman, who they said acted alone and did not have a criminal history but whose mother had worked as an administrative assistant in the Annunciation school’s business office.

The assailant’s name was legally changed from Robert to Robin about five years ago because Westman “identifies as a female and wants her name to reflect that identification,” according to court records.

Police have disclosed few details about the three weapons Westman carried Wednesday but confirmed they were purchased legally and “recently.”

Elected leaders in the overwhelmingly Democratic Twin Cities said the shooting was just the latest example of the deadly consequences of a society awash in guns.

Even though Minnesota is home to some of the toughest firearm laws in the country, advocates said more must be done to prevent both high-profile mass shootings and the gun violence that unfolds every day, away from the spotlight.

“I beg you, I ask you to please pray but don’t stop with your words,” said DeBoer, the school principal. “Let’s make a difference and support this community, these families, these teachers. Never again can we let this happen.”

Frey was more pointed in his remarks to reporters earlier Wednesday, dismissing offers of “thoughts and prayers” as insufficient to a familiar tragedy.

“Don’t just say this is about thoughts and prayers right now,” he said. “These kids were literally praying. … They should be able to go to school or church in peace, without the fear or risk of violence.”

Little Ayla’s father is among those parents furious with politicians who continue to block gun-control measures despite shootings like the one his daughter lived through Wednesday.

“The American political sphere allows this to happen over and over and over again,” Turner said. “There’s a problem of a culture of violence in America.”

His family has now experienced that firsthand. And even in the security of her home Wednesday afternoon, the little girl seemed to be alternating between fear and something close to her normal self, he said.

They were sitting together in the living room, doors and windows thrown open on a beautiful late-August afternoon, when Ayla turned to her dad and asked him to shut it all, to lock the house down.

Kaur reported from Washington, and Thebault reported from Los Angeles. Michelle Boorstein, Aaron Schaffer and Gaya Gupta in Washington, Molly Hennessy-Fiske in Houston and Grace Moon in Seoul contributed to this report.
item.author: Hannah Knowles, Sheila Regan, Anumita Kaur, Reis Thebault

item.title: 2 children killed, 17 people injured at Minneapolis Catholic school Mass
item.description:
This live coverage has ended.

Police have identified a suspect in a shooting Wednesday that killed two children and injured more than a dozen other people at a Catholic school in Minneapolis. Robin Westman, 23, began shooting through the windows of Annunciation Church on the city’s southwest side around 8:30 a.m. local time, police said. Children from the adjacent Annunciation Catholic School were attending Mass. An 8-year-old and a 10-year-old were killed while sitting in pews, authorities said, and the shooter died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Fourteen children and three adults were injured; all are expected to survive. The private school enrolls children from preschool through eighth grade. The FBI is investigating the matter as domestic terrorism and a hate crime targeting Catholics, FBI Director Kash Patel said. Minneapolis police chief Brian O’Hara said investigators were reviewing a “manifesto” posted by the shooter.

Children prayed for ‘a future filled with hope.’ Then the gunfire began.

By Hannah Knowles, Sheila Regan, Anumita Kaur and Reis Thebault

MINNEAPOLIS — The children filed into the pews of Annunciation Catholic Church on Wednesday morning for their first Mass of the new school year, a time of nervous energy and excitement.

But just minutes into the service, as the students were reciting Psalm 139 — a call-and-answer prayer about God’s all-knowing love — the sound of gunfire ripped through the air and the church windows shattered. In an instant, the back-to-school glee dissolved into terror and chaos.

This is an excerpt from a full story. Wednesday, August 27, 2025 9:21 PM EDT

Gun rights YouTuber responds to being named in shooter’s manifesto

By Praveena Somasundaram and Chris Dehghanpoor

Brandon Herrera, a gun rights YouTuber who is running to represent Texas in Congress, said he was “disgusted” that the Minneapolis shooter mentioned him in their manifesto.

The assailant timed a manifesto to be posted on YouTube to coincide with the attack, officials said. In an 11-minute video, Robin Westman said he met Herrera at a gun trade show last year, and they “agreed on a lot of things” during a brief conversation.

“Brandon Herrera for president,” Westman said in the video, which has since been taken down.

In a statement, Herrera said he did not remember Westman from the “thousands of people” he met at the show, held annually in Las Vegas. He added that he would speak with law enforcement if needed.

“I’m still physically sickened and angry about this clearly hate motivated attack on innocent children,” he said.

Herrera, who competed in the Republican primary for Texas’s 23rd Congressional District last year, entered the race for the seat again this month.



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 9:04 PM EDT

Podcast: ‘I got down and ran’

By Elahe Izadi

Parents frantically rushed to Annunciation Catholic School in Minneapolis on Wednesday to reunite with their children. Brooks Turner picked up his 4-year-old daughter, Ayla, who was in a preschool classroom in the church basement when the shooting began

Ayla sat next to Turner as he explained what happened. It had sounded like “somebody was trying to break down the ceiling above them,” he said. Ayla added, “I got down and ran.”

On today’s Post Reports, Turner shares this story, and reporter Kim Bellware walks through what we’ve learned about the shooting and how the tragic event fits into the nation’s history of gun violence.



By Angie Orellana Hernandez

The shooter was employed for “several months” this year at a cannabis dispensary in Minnesota called RISE Dispensary, a spokesperson for the company confirmed in a statement. Westman was not an employee at the time of the shooting.

RISE said it is cooperating with police.

“Our priority is to respect the investigative process, to extend our deepest sympathies to all those impacted, and support our team through this horrific tragedy,” the company said.

Wednesday, August 27, 2025 8:24 PM EDT

Shooter posted rambling video manifesto

By Justin Jouvenal and Chris Dehghanpoor

The 23-year-old shooter who opened fire at a Catholic school in Minneapolis on Wednesday posted rambling videos to YouTube showing reverence for other mass shooters, gun magazines scrawled with “Kill Donald Trump” and racial slurs, and messages apologizing to family members.

This is an excerpt from a full story.

Wednesday, August 27, 2025 8:06 PM EDT

A sixth-grader and her family are ‘trying to put the pieces together’

By Anumita Kaur

Vincent Francoual, 57, had just dropped off his daughter at Annunciation Catholic School on Wednesday when he got a text from his wife: There had been a shooting.

He raced back to the school, about three blocks from the family’s home, on autopilot.

“I was incredulous,” he said. “I didn’t really realize what was going on.”

His 11-year-old daughter, Chloe Francoual, was safe, and Francoual and his wife reunited with her at the school’s gym, where families were gathering after the incident. His daughter, who was in the church when the shooting happened, was inconsolable.

“We just cried and asked, ‘Are you okay?’” Francoual recalled.

He added: “She saw kids bleeding. She saw kids on the floor. She ran to the downstairs area. She put a table against the door.”

The sixth-graders are assigned second-grade buddies, and Francoual said his daughter is racked with guilt that she didn’t take her second-grade buddy with her. That child was later determined to be safe.

“When your daughter tells you that she really thought she was going to die … I don’t know. I don’t know what to say to that,” Francoual said. He’s still trying to understand what happened through her eyes. “We’re trying to put the pieces together right now.”

Francoual, a local chef, has been living in Minneapolis since 1998 and immigrated from France. He loves the city, and his daughter adores the school. Their neighborhood is close-knit, with people frequently stopping to say hello on the street, and their school’s community is like a family, he said.

Sometimes, Francoual and his wife joke that they will move back to France. Their daughter usually throws a fit, insisting she loves her school and Minneapolis, he said.

“Today, on the way out of this, she said, ‘We gotta go. We gotta move to France,’” Francoual said.



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 7:33 PM EDT

Chicago archbishop calls for lawmakers to act on gun control

By Michelle Boorstein

Cardinal Blase Cupich, archbishop of Chicago, forcefully called for changes to gun legislation and criticized recent GOP-led federal budget cuts.

Considered an ideological ally of Popes Francis and Leo, Cupich urged U.S. leaders to “make the safety of our people a national priority.”

“The facts are clear,” Cupich, who was appointed to his post in 2014, said in a statement. “Guns are plentiful and common sense attempts to limit their availability have been largely rejected in the name of a freedom not found in our constitution. Cutbacks in funding for health care and social service programs will only exacerbate a national mental health crisis and increase alienation.”

Cupich exhorted elected officials to take action so parents can send their children to school without fear that they might face gunfire.

“Surely they must be moved by these shootings,” Cupich said of the officials. “We pray that they will not see them as inevitable because then we will have certainly surrendered our rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. Please pray and please act. Now.”

By Praveena Somasundaram

Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D) ordered flags to fly at half-staff indefinitely to honor the lives of the two children killed, calling the shooting a tragedy that “brought devastation to a place that should be a safe space for children to learn.”



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 6:31 PM EDT

10-year-old describes how friend protected him during shooting

By Gaya Gupta

Morning Mass had barely begun when 10-year-old Weston Halsne, a fifth-grade student at Annunciation, heard the first shots fired. He was sitting just two seats away from the church’s stained glass windows that police believe the shooter fired through.

“The shots were right next to me,” Weston told NBC affiliate station KARE.

His school held shooting drills roughly every month to prepare for such a situation at school, but never at church, he said. He joined his classmates Wednesday in ducking under the pews and covering his head. His friend Victor tried to protect him by lying on top of him during the shooting and was shot in the back, Weston said.

“I was super scared for him, but I think now he’s okay,” Weston told the television station, later adding: “He’s really brave.”



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 6:10 PM EDT

Minnesota has tightened its gun laws in recent years. Officials say it’s not enough.

By Kim Bellware, Amy B Wang and Patrick Svitek

Minnesota has some of the nation’s toughest gun laws — but many of the state’s leading Democrats said Wednesday that the deadly shooting in Minneapolis showed a need for stricter regulations nationwide.

Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D) said on MSNBC argued that her party keeps “getting thwarted” in its efforts to reduce gun violence, while the head of the state’s Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party, Richard Colborn, said that “all options must be on the table to end gun violence.”

And Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey opened a news conference Wednesday with pointed remarks dismissing offers of “thoughts and prayers” from Republicans. “Don’t say this is about thoughts and prayers right now,” Frey said. “These kids were literally praying.”

Gov. Tim Walz (D), a gun owner whose onetime “A” rating by the National Rifle Association changed to an “F” after he embraced gun regulations, has signed several bills in recent years that have strengthened the state’s gun laws.

They include legislation in 2023 requiring universal background checks and an “Extreme Risk Protection Order” or “red flag” law that allows law enforcement to temporarily remove guns from a person deemed to be a danger to themselves or others. The state has the seventh-lowest rate of gun deaths in the nation, according to Giffords, the nonprofit gun violence prevention research group.

Still, Frey, who has advocated for measures like a statewide assault weapon ban, called on elected officials to “recognize that we have more guns in this country than we have people.”

Minneapolis police have disclosed few details about the three weapons the shooter used on Wednesday but confirmed they were purchased legally and “recently.”

By Angie Orellana Hernandez

Children’s Minnesota Hospital-Minneapolis said four shooting victims had been discharged as of Wednesday afternoon. Three children remained hospitalized there.



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 5:27 PM EDT

Minnesota’s congressional delegation shares grief over shooting

By Anumita Kaur

Members of Congress representing Minnesota shared grief and shock Wednesday as news of the shooting unfolded.

“It’s the first week of school,” Sen. Tina Smith (D) said. “These kids should not be fearing for their lives.”

Rep. Brad Finstad (R) thanked law enforcement for their response, and Rep. Betty McCollum (D) said she was devastated to learn that children were targeted at Mass. Rep. Ilhan Omar (D), whose district includes Minneapolis, said she is praying for the families and will continue to monitor the situation.

“I am heartbroken by the horrific violence at Annunciation Catholic School in Minneapolis this morning,” Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D) said .



By Anumita Kaur

It’s unclear when classes will resume at Annunciation Catholic School.

“As we process and navigate this unfathomable time together, we will be in touch this weekend regarding when school will resume,” the school said in a statement Wednesday. “Investigators and others are still on campus doing their essential work and we expect this to continue for some time.”

Wednesday, August 27, 2025 4:50 PM EDT

Church shooting upends quiet neighborhood

By Hannah Knowles

The shooting upended a quiet residential neighborhood that people love for its walkable streets, Kowalski’s grocery store and old-growth trees.

Neighbors hear bells ringing from Annunciation Church and the adjacent Catholic school throughout the day, said Laura Kirstein, who lives about a block away and has friends who have sent their kids there.

Kirstein, 55, watched in horror Wednesday morning as parents ran toward the school to look for their children. She walked across the street to a neighbor, and they hugged and cried for several minutes. “We didn’t let go,” she said.



By Kim Bellware

The three firearms used by the shooter were purchased legally and “recently,” said Minneapolis Police Chief Brian O’Hara, who declined to specify an exact date of purchase.



By Anumita Kaur

Minneapolis Police Chief Brian O’Hara said there is no information on the shooter’s motive as of Wednesday afternoon.

“There was some sort of manifesto that was timed to come out on YouTube,” which has been taken down, O’Hara said.

Officials are investigating that and have three search warrants for residential locations. These efforts should help officials understand the shooter’s motive, he said.

By Aaron Schaffer

Westman’s name was legally changed to Robin in January 2020 after their mother filed an application in November 2019 on their behalf to change it. Westman, who also signed the application, “identifies as a female and wants her name to reflect that identification,” a court order signed by Judge Tanya O. O’Brien reads.



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 4:11 PM EDT

Shooter’s father lives near school

By Sheila Regan

The shooter’s father, James Allen Westman, lives with his second wife within a mile of Annunciation Catholic School.

Jim White, a neighbor who lives across the street from the couple, said they had a blended family with children from previous marriages — he estimated about five children ranging from teen to adult. He wasn’t sure how many of the young people lived there with the parents.

“They’re really nice people, always really good neighbors,” White said. “This doesn’t make sense.”

This morning, White said six police cars parked outside of the Westman home while helicopters flew overhead. White watched the scene through his window.

“Jim came out with hands up,” White said, adding that Westman’s wife also had her hands up outside. He was unsure what happened to them after that.



By Angie Orellana Hernandez

All the victims reported injured in the shooting are expected to survive and have been reunited with family members, Minneapolis Police Chief Brian O’Hara said.

The victims have a “range of injuries,” O’Hara said.

By Angie Orellana Hernandez

Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey (D) condemned attacks on transgender people amid reports that the shooter had undergone a name change.

“Anybody who is using this as an opportunity to villainize our trans community or any other community out there has lost their sense of common humanity,” Frey said during a news conference. “Kids died today, this needs to be about them.”



By Anumita Kaur

Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D) and Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey (D) both urged action against gun violence.

“We can’t just say this shouldn’t happen again and then allow it to happen again,” Frey said during a news conference Wednesday afternoon. “We have to be doing more than talking. … The impetus has to be on us leaders to do more.”



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 3:36 PM EDT

FBI identifies shooter, calls attack domestic terrorism

By Angie Orellana Hernandez

The Annunciation Church shooter was identified as Robin Westman, FBI director Kash Patel wrote on X.

Patel said the FBI is investigating the shooting as an act of domestic terrorism and a hate crime targeting Catholics.

By John Woodrow Cox, Steven Rich, Lucas Trevor, John Muyskens and Monica Ulmanu

There have been seven school-related shootings this year that killed one student and injured seven others. Those incidents spanned the country, occurring in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina, Mississippi, Texas, Michigan and Washington state.



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 3:18 PM EDT

Community rushes to help after shooting: ‘It breaks your heart’

By Hannah Knowles

People from around the Minneapolis area rushed to the scene hoping to make themselves helpful. Alberto Gurrieri, a pastor at Twin Cities Bible Church, an evangelical church in St. Paul, drove over and peered over the yellow police tape toward Annunciation Church about a block away.

“I wanted to see if there was any people I could pray with,” he said.

A drone floated overhead.

“It breaks your heart,” said Gurrieri, 31. “You’re talking about children, talking about their first week of school, and we’re talking about the effects of sin and death in this world.”

“It makes you cry out to the lord,” he said.



By Ben Brasch

Pope Leo XIV expressed “his heartfelt condolences and the assurance of spiritual closeness to all those affected by this terrible tragedy, especially the families now grieving the loss of a child,” according to the Vatican’s news site.

He also offered in the telegram a papal blessing to the people of the Twin Cities.

By Kim Bellware

One adult and six children remain in critical condition at the Hennepin County Medical Center, the hospital said in an update Wednesday afternoon. Another child and an adult are being treated for non-life-threatening injuries. Children’s Minnesota Hospital-Minneapolis was treating seven children between 9 and 16 years old and had discharged one as of Wednesday afternoon.



By Anumita Kaur

“We can’t allow ourselves to become numb to mass shootings,” former president Barack Obama wrote on X Wednesday. “What happened today in Minneapolis is heartbreaking, and Michelle and I are praying for the parents who have lost a child or will be sitting at their hospital bedside after yet another act of unspeakable, unnecessary violence.”



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 2:23 PM EDT

Kids with crayons and tearful parents in reunification hall

By Hannah Knowles

Howard Dotson, a 54-year-old chaplain in Minneapolis, rushed to the site of the shooting to help after seeing an “armada” of police cars head over.

He waited with a parent at the perimeter law enforcement had set up around Annunciation Catholic School, then went to a hall where families were being reunited with their children, he said. Kids appeared to be in shock. Mothers were crying.

He passed out crayons and markers for the children to draw, he said, because that helps with trauma.

A teacher told him that students sang “Lord Prepare Me to be a Sanctuary” as they made their way from the chapel to the reunification hall.

He said he helps PTSD victims through a group called Trauma Recovery Services and has worked with several police departments over the years.

By Natalie Allison

President Donald Trump has signed a proclamation honoring the victims of the school shooting in Minneapolis, ordering American flags to be flown at half-staff on public grounds through Sunday night. He called it “a mark of respect for the victims of the senseless acts of violence” Wednesday.



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 1:59 PM EDT

Photos: Students and parents evacuate after shooting

By Max Becherer

A parent hugs their child during an active shooter situation at the Annunciation Church in Minneapolis on Wednesday.

Families and loved ones walk outside the police barricades after the shooting at the church, which is also home to an elementary school.

A person walks out of the school as police respond.



By Anumita Kaur

The Minneapolis division of the FBI is investigating the shooting at Annunciation Catholic Church alongside local officials, the agency said in a social media statement.

“The FBI will devote every available resource to support this ongoing investigative effort,” said Alvin M. Winston Sr., special agent in charge of the FBI’s Minneapolis division.

Wednesday, August 27, 2025 1:22 PM EDT

A quiet neighborhood faces tragedy

By Hannah Knowles

Annunciation Catholic School is surrounded by homes in a quiet, tree-filled neighborhood. A big welcome sign hangs on the brick school building, saying: “A future filled with HOPE.”

The rush of parents looking for their children is over; journalists are camped out by yellow police tape.



By Hannah Knowles

FBI agents are knocking on the doors of homes around Annunciation Catholic School, gathering information. One agent asked a woman if she has noticed any strange cars in the neighborhood.



By Sheila Regan

Madie Brandt was on her way to work Wednesday morning when her car was swarmed with police cars and ambulances at 8:44 a.m. “Cops were flying down the street,” she said.

Amid the chaos, her car is now stuck in the blocked-off zone of law enforcement and first-responder vehicles. Brandt said she saw a woman jump out of her car and call out, “Where are my kids?”

Wednesday, August 27, 2025 12:42 PM EDT

4 patients need surgery and 7 are in critical condition after shooting, hospital says

By Sheila Regan

Hennepin County Medical Center was mobilizing its resources for the second of two mass casualty events in the past 24 hours, its chair of emergency medicine Dr. Thomas E. Wyatt said at a news conference.

The facility, a level 1 trauma center, is treating two adults and nine children between the ages of 6 and 14 from the Annunciation School shooting, Wyatt said. Four patients needed the operating room, and seven — all children — are in critical condition. HCMC has not had casualties with them, Wyatt said.

“I just want to say how proud I am to work for this organization,” Wyatt said.

“We see a lot of gun shot wounds throughout the year,” he added. “It does take a toll.”



By Michelle Boorstein and Tim Meko

Joe Ruff, editor in chief of the archdiocese’s newspaper, The Catholic Spirit, said Wednesday was the third day of school at Annunciation. The students, who run from preschool to 8th grade, he said, were at an all-school Mass when the shooting happened.

Annunciation parish was founded in 1922, he said, and the school opened the next year. In 2013, the parish merged with another parish, called Visitation.



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 12:23 PM EDT

Gunman shot at children through church windows, police chief says

By Gaya Gupta

The gunman approached the church around 8:30 a.m. local time during a Mass at the Annunciation Church and began firing a rifle through the windows toward the children in the pews, Minneapolis Police Chief Brian O’Hara said.

“He was absolutely shooting outside of the building, on the side of the church," O’Hara said. He said it appeared that the gunman may have gone inside the church, “but I don’t believe we’ve located any casings inside the building.”

The gunman then killed himself in the parking lot, O’Hara said. He said police believe the suspect acted alone and that he was in his early 20s and does not have a known criminal history.

“We are looking through information left behind to try and determine some type of motive,” he said.

Wednesday, August 27, 2025 12:22 PM EDT

Trump calls Walz to offer condolences

By Dylan Wells

President Donald Trump called Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz after the shooting to offer his condolences to the people of Minnesota, and Walz thanked him for the support, according to a person aware of the call who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a private conversation.

Trump did not reach out to Walz earlier this summer after a gunman killed a top Democratic lawmaker and her husband and wounded another legislator and his wife in a politically motivated attack. Trump asked at the time why he would call Walz and attacked the 2024 Democratic vice-presidential nominee.



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 12:18 PM EDT

A series of shots and sprint to school

By Hannah Knowles

A block from the church, Carla Maldonado broke into tears as she hugged another woman.

“He’s okay, he’s okay,” Maldonado told her.

“Let me know if you need anything,” the other woman said.

“Thank you,” Maldonado said through sobs, her young son and daughter beside her in their school uniforms.

Maldonado said she lives in the area and heard the gunshots. She sprinted to the school, saw orange smoke around the church and then ran into a friend.

“He’s got a gun,” the friend said, and they ran inside the friend’s house. They called 911, but couldn’t immediately get through.

All-school mass was underway when the shooting began, Maldonado said. “Somebody had to know that all the school was going to be in church at this time … how can that be random?” she asked.

Maldonado’s son and daughter remembered a barrage of gunshots — how many, they were not sure. Kids screamed and cried and hid under the pews, they said.



By Gaya Gupta

Minneapolis Police Chief Brian O’Hara said the gunman had a rifle, a shotgun and a pistol and fired inside the church from all three weapons. He said that he could not confirm whether he was lawfully carrying those weapons, or how exactly many rounds were fired, but said it was “in the dozens.”

By Gaya Gupta and Kim Bellware

Minneapolis Police Chief Brian O’Hara said two children, ages 8 and 10, were killed, and 17 others were injured, 14 of them children.

The two deceased children were “killed where they sat in the pews” while attending a back-to-school mass, O’Hara said.



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 12:03 PM EDT

Minneapolis mayor: ‘Children are dead’

By Gaya Gupta

Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey (D), now speaking at a news conference, confirmed that children were killed in the attack.

“Don’t just say this is about thoughts and prayers right now. These kids were literally praying,” he said. “It was the first week of school. They were in a church. These are kids that should be learning with their friends. They should be playing on the playground. They should be able to go to school or church in peace, without the fear or risk of violence. And their parents should have the same kind of assurance. These are the sort of basic assurances that every family should have every step of the day, regardless of where they are in our country.”



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 11:53 AM EDT

Photos: Law enforcement responds to a suspected shooter

By Hannah Knowles

Law enforcement responds to a suspected shooter at the Annunciation Church on Minneapolis’s southwest side on Wednesday.

By Gaya Gupta

Agents from the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives are on the scene and assisting local authorities, bureau spokesperson Ashlee Sherrill told The Washington Post.

“If there are any firearms that are recovered at the scene, ATF will certainly conduct a trace on those to help aid the investigation,” she said.

The Department of Homeland Security is also monitoring the situation and is in touch with its interagency partners, Secretary Kristi L. Noem wrote on social media.



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 11:47 AM EDT

Students and neighbors in shock after shooting

By Sheila Regan

Helicopters continue to swarm overhead in the area, with police having closed a five-block radius around the church and school.

The elementary school-age children appeared shaken as they were escorted by their parents away from the school. One young girl said she heard the shots from another part of the building. “It was during mass,” she said.

Margaret Richards, a neighbor in the area whose now-adult children attended the church school when they were little, walked over when she heard the news.

“I’m sick to my stomach,” she said. “I can’t believe this is happening. This is a very small community, that’s why people pick the school.”



By Hannah Knowles

Brooks Turner, 35, held his preschooler daughter Ayla in his arms as he walked away from the scene. Turner said he was told students were in church for an all-school Mass when the shooting started — but Ayla and the other pre-K students were in a room below. Ayla said she heard banging and hid in a play kitchen before she was evacuated.

By Gaya Gupta

Hennepin County Medical Center, a Level 1 trauma hospital in Minneapolis, confirmed it is caring for multiple victims of the shooting at Annunciation Catholic School. It said it will provide an update on patients at noon Eastern at a news conference outside the hospital’s trauma center entrance, on South 8th & Park Avenue.



By Kim Bellware

Six patients from the shooting have been transferred to Children’s Minnesota — Minneapolis Hospital, a hospital spokesperson told the Washington Post, adding that they would not confirm the children’s conditions at the time. Children’s Minnesota is the primary Level I pediatric trauma center in the area.



By Emily Davies

President Donald Trump has been briefed on the Minneapolis shooting, he said Wednesday morning on Truth Social.

“The FBI quickly responded and they are on the scene,” he wrote. “The White House will continue to monitor this terrible situation. Please join me in praying for everyone involved!”

By Gaya Gupta

A news briefing on the shooting will be held at noon Eastern, a spokesperson for the city of Minneapolis said in a statement. It will be live-streamed here.



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 11:04 AM EDT

Families rush to Minneapolis school after reports of shooting

By Hannah Knowles

Family members of students at Annunciation Catholic School and neighbors rushed to the scene, which police had cordoned off with vehicles and yellow tape. Parents walked away Wednesday clutching the hands of young children in school uniforms — green tops and plaid skirts or khaki pants.

Rachel Anderson, who was dog-sitting nearby, said she heard a barrage of gunshots and thought, at first, that someone was doing work on their house. Neighbors began to call 911 but struggled to get though — apparently because there were so many calls.

Anderson went to see what was happening and watched kids, sobbing, leave the school, followed by their teachers.

“You could hear all the kids just sobbing and crying, and then the parents were coming and they’re frantic,” Anderson said.

The shooting makes her “angry” that elected officials are focused on other issues such as transgender people instead of gun violence, she said.



Wednesday, August 27, 2025 10:58 AM EDT

Suspected shooter at Minneapolis school is ‘contained,’ officials say

By Kim Bellware

The suspected shooter at the Annunciation Catholic School on Minneapolis’s southwest side was “contained” early Wednesday as a police situation remained ongoing, Minneapolis city officials said in a statement via social media just before 9:30 a.m. Central time.

City officials said there was no active threat to the wider community and advised residents to avoid the area around the church to make way for first responders helping victims, whose statuses were unclear Wednesday morning.

Families of children at the school were directed to a reunification zone established at the school.

By Kim Bellware

Annunciation Catholic School is a K-8 private school near the Tangletown area on Minneapolis’s southwest side. Next door to the school is Annunciation Catholic Church.



By Gaya Gupta

Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey posted on social media that he is “monitoring reports of horrific violence in South Minneapolis” and is in touch with his emergency response team and the city’s police chief, Brian O’Hara.



By Kim Bellware

The FBI had agents “en route” to the shooting scene, Deputy Director Dan Bongino confirmed Wednesday morning via social media.

item.title: ICE asks for access to Chicago-area Navy base to assist operations
item.description:
The request followed Homeland Security Secretary Kristi L. Noem’s declaration that a “strike team” of immigration enforcement agents would arrive in Chicago soon.

The Trump administration wants to use a Navy base north of Chicago as a launchpad for federal law enforcement activity against undocumented immigration, defense officials said Tuesday, as the White House contemplates also deploying thousands of U.S. troops to the nation’s third-largest city amid rising tension with the Illinois governor.

Officials at Naval Station Great Lakes on Wednesday acknowledged having received a request from the Department of Homeland Security that seeks “limited support” for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, whose aggressive tactics under the current administration have drawn outrage from opponents of President Donald Trump. The base, a hub for recruit training, would provide “facilities, infrastructure, and other logistical needs” if the request is granted, defense officials said in a statement.

No decisions to approve access have been made, officials said. That responsibility lies with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who since taking office in January has eagerly pledged the Pentagon’s full cooperation as DHS and its agents search for, detain and remove undocumented immigrants. He has approved the use of other military bases to build detention facilities for people in DHS custody.

The White House is determined to ramp up ICE operations, with Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller pressing for 3,000 arrests per day. The polarizing strategy has strained DHS, prompted public outcry and set off numerous legal battles.

Asked about its plans for the Navy base in Illinois, DHS tied the discussion to Trump’s call for safer cities, though the vast majority of those targeted for removal have no history of violent crime. Homeland Security Secretary Kristi L. Noem said in an interview with NewsNation this week that DHS will have an “ICE strike team” in Chicago soon.

“Across the country, DHS law enforcement are arresting and removing the worst of worst including gang members, murderers, pedophiles, and rapists that have terrorized American communities,” the agency said in a statement.

Spokespeople for Hegseth referred questions to DHS.

The request for use of Naval Station Great Lakes was reported earlier by the Chicago Sun-Times, which cited an email the base’s commanding officer, Navy Capt. Stephen Yargosz, sent to staff. Yargosz said in the message that DHS authorities would be at the Navy base from Sept. 2 to 30, with a “potential to also support National Guard units.”

The Washington Post reported Saturday that military officials have for many weeks been devising plans to send U.S. troops to Chicago, likely coordinated with expanded ICE operations there. A range of options exist, with one likely plan calling for a few thousand members of the National Guard to deploy, officials familiar with the matter said. The deployment of active-duty troops has also been considered, officials said.

The backlash from state and local officials has been fierce. Gov. JB Pritzker (D) has said that while Chicago has some challenges, there are no circumstances that warrant the deployment of military force there.

Pritzker told reporters Wednesday that no one from the White House or elsewhere in the federal government had contacted him about the matter.

“They don’t seem to want to communicate at all. And that’s odd because it sounds like what they’re trying to do is march right over local police,” Pritzker said of the Trump administration. “You know, we used to hear that the president of the United States supported local police. We support local police. But now it appears that he wants to ignore them all together and just do whatever he has a whim about on that day.”

Pritzker and Trump have traded jabs in recent days, with Trump saying he wants the governor to approve a military deployment. But the president suggested, too, that he may send the military even if Pritzker does not endorse the move. Trump, speaking Tuesday, claimed he has “the right to do anything that I want to do.”

“I’m the president of the United States,” he said. “If I think our country is in danger — and it is in danger in these cities — I can do it.”

Pritzker quickly responded on social media: “No, Donald. You can’t do whatever you want.”

Experts on constitutional law questioned the legal limits of what Trump can approve, while acknowledging that he may pursue another domestic military deployment anyway and let the courts sort it out later.

Elizabeth Goitein, senior director of the Brennan Center’s Liberty and National Security Program, said that for Trump to deploy the Illinois National Guard in Chicago without Pritzker’s consent, he could rely on the same legal authority laid out in Title 10 of U.S. code to send troops to Los Angeles earlier this year.

In that case, the administration cited a section of law that says that U.S. troops are allowed to deploy within the United States with a limited role when “there is a rebellion or a danger of a rebellion against the authority of the Government” or when the president is unable to “execute the laws of the United States.” Administration officials cited a handful of protesters throwing concrete at ICE agents as the legal basis for the deployment.

Whether the administration met the legal bar for the deployment in California remains contested, with a trial held earlier this month in U.S. District Court and no ruling issued yet by Judge Charles Breyer.

But even if that deployment is deemed to have been lawful, the situation in Chicago is separate and there is no indication of a rebellion there, Goiten said. Violent street crime also cannot be used as a legal basis to send in U.S. troops, she said.

“The administration,” she said, “will be on even thinner legal ice in Chicago than they are in Los Angeles.”

Marianne LeVine contributed to this report.
item.author: Dan Lamothe

item.title: Alligator Alcatraz being emptied of immigrant detainees, Florida says
item.description:
The plan is for the number to dwindle to zero this week, eight weeks after the controversial facility opened in the Everglades.

Two months after it opened, the controversial immigrant detention center hastily erected in the middle of the Everglades is losing all of its detainees, a state official said in an email.

Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) said Wednesday that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security has “increased the pace of the removals” from Alligator Alcatraz, but he did not comment on the facility possibly being emptied entirely of detainees after a federal judge ruled last week that the site must be dismantled by late October.

In an email obtained by The Washington Post on Wednesday, Florida Division of Emergency Management Director Kevin Guthrie said that “we are probably going to be down to 0 individuals within a few days.”

Guthrie was responding to an inquiry Friday from people who wanted to provide chaplaincy services at the detention camp.

“I think he was just referring to they’re deporting them very quickly, and that’s a good thing,” DeSantis said of Guthrie’s email. “We don’t determine who goes into the facility. ... Who they send in or don’t send in is on their decision.”

DeSantis said the “rapid removals from Alligator Alcatraz” by the Department of Homeland Security may be a result of the court ruling. DHS confirmed that the department is moving detainees out of the Everglades site.

DHS spokesman Nathaniel Madden said that despite what he called an “activist judge” who ordered the facility to be dismantled, “we are working at turbo speed on cost-effective and innovative ways to deliver on the American people’s mandate for mass deportations of criminal illegal aliens.”

“DHS is complying with this order and moving detainees to other facilities. We will continue to fight tooth-and-nail to remove the worst of the worst from American streets,” Madden said in an email.

Opponents who have kept vigils outside the gates of the facility since it opened on July 1 said busloads of detainees were being moved out last weekend. A congressman who visited the center last week said fewer than 350 men remained at a place that DeSantis said could eventually hold 5,000 people.

The DeSantis administration seized acres of land around an old airstrip under an immigration emergency order the governor first issued in 2023 and has renewed every year since. He said the state was working in conjunction with DHS to deport immigrants arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents and Florida law enforcement officers assisting ICE.

The relocation of the detained immigrants comes six days after a federal judge in Miami ordered the state to wind down operations in the Everglades as a result of a lawsuit filed by environmentalists and the Miccosukee Tribe of Indians.

“This is a detention center that never should have opened,” said Tania Galloni, an attorney with Earthjustice.

Earthjustice and Friends of the Everglades sued the state and federal governments for erecting the facility without first doing an environmental assessment.

“It’s gratifying that operations have come to a close there because every day that center operated, it was causing environmental harm,” Galloni said.

Guthrie did not respond to a request for comment.

Guthrie’s department, which is usually deployed to help the state prepare for and recover from hurricanes, used contractors and spent at least $218 million to build the temporary site on a little-used airstrip in the Big Cypress National Preserve. It took only eight days to put up “soft-sided tents” around chain-link cages. The site, which is near the border of Everglades National Park, has no electricity or plumbing. It’s being run on generators that power portable air conditioners and lighting and has portable toilets.

Drinking and bathing water is trucked in several times a day, and sewage and other waste must be trucked out.

“This is a major victory for Florida’s environment and due process,” said state Rep. Anna Eskamani (D-Orlando), who testified in the case on environmental impacts. “I’ve said it before and will say it again, no one should be detained in the middle of the Florida Everglades. Not only is it environmentally unsound, but it’s inhumane.”

Two separate lawsuits over the treatment of detainees and their access to attorneys are ongoing.
item.author: Lori Rozsa

item.title: Man gets 89 days in prison, for every day he faked death to leave wife
item.description:
Wisconsin man Ryan Borgwardt faked his drowning with an overturned kayak to establish a new life in Eastern Europe with a woman he met online, prosecutors said.

A Wisconsin man who faked his death and fled overseas to be with a woman he met online, leaving his wife and children behind, was convicted of obstructing an officer and sentenced to 89 days in jail.

The sentence’s length is equal to the number of days Ryan Borgwardt, 45, “obstructed law enforcement” as he built a new life in the country of Georgia last year while authorities back home searched for him, Judge Mark T. Slate said Tuesday in court in Green Lake County. Officials initially believed that Borgwardt had drowned in a lake, but they came to suspect that he was alive after they found out Canadian authorities had run his name in the days after he disappeared.

“For the defendant, and anyone else who is thinking about faking their death: If you persist in your deception, the longer you obstruct, the longer you are [duplicitous] instead of coming forward and admitting your mistake, the longer the penalty should be,” Slate said.

Under the terms of a plea agreement, the state’s prosecutor requested a sentence of 45 days in prison. But Slate nearly doubled that — stating that 89 days elapsed between when Borgwardt was reported missing and when authorities made contact with him — and said he hoped the more severe punishment would deter anyone thinking of committing a similar crime.

Borgwardt pleaded no contest to the charges against him. Before his sentence was announced, he briefly addressed the court, saying, “I deeply regret the actions that I did that night and all the pain that I caused my family and friends.”

Borgwardt was reported missing on Aug. 12, 2024, after his family said he didn’t return from a kayak trip to Green Lake in central Wisconsin the night before. Officers from the Green Lake County Sheriff’s Office found several clues in and around the lake that suggested Borgwardt may have drowned, including an overturned kayak, his phone, and his fishing pole and tackle box containing his ID, according to the criminal complaint.

Local and regional authorities and community groups deployed extensive resources to search for Borgwardt, including fishermen, sonars and cadaver dogs, while his wife and three children were “left to believe that he was missing, or worse, dead,” Green Lake County District Attorney Gerise LaSpisa said Tuesday in court. After 58 days without finding a body, investigators started digging into Borgwardt’s background and discovered a search for his name by Canadian Border Patrol. They inspected his laptop and found that he had been communicating with a woman in Uzbekistan before his disappearance and had made inquiries about moving money to a foreign bank, Green Lake County Sheriff Mark Podoll said at a news conference in November. Borgwardt also allegedly replaced the hard drive on his laptop before the kayaking trip.

At that point, investigators began to suspect that Borgwardt was still alive and had fled the country. They contacted him by email on Nov. 8, 2024, and he returned to the United States to face trial, 121 days after he was reported missing. His wife of 22 years filed for divorce shortly thereafter, the Associated Press reported.

Borgwardt’s lawyer, Erik C. Johnson, told the court that his client was deeply remorseful and “taking responsibility for his actions.” Johnson said Borgwardt didn’t have to come back to the United States because his crime was a “non-extraditable misdemeanor,” and he argued that Borgwardt’s voluntary return showed that he “wanted to make amends.”

Johnson did not immediately respond to a request for further comment Wednesday morning.

LaSpisa said Borgwardt’s disappearance was a carefully planned scheme to allow him to “disappear from his everyday life of being a husband and father in Wisconsin.” She said he made “extensive” preparations for his disappearance in the months before the kayaking trip: researching drownings and “how to successfully disappear”; taking out “a sizable life insurance policy”; transferring money overseas; and applying for a replacement passport, claiming his original one was lost or stolen, though his wife later found it in their safe.

In the period before Borgwardt’s disappearance, LaSpisa said, he regularly communicated with the woman he met online, “professing his love and desire to create a new life with her,” and reversed his vasectomy.

Borgwardt told investigators that on the day he disappeared, he took a kayak out on Green Lake and brought a child-size inflatable boat with him. After flipping the kayak and dumping his phone in the water, he paddled the inflatable boat to shore, got on an e-bike that he had stashed at the boat launch and rode through the night to Madison, some 70 miles away, according to the complaint. There, he said, he boarded a bus to Detroit, crossed the Canadian border to Toronto Pearson International Airport, and flew to Paris and then to an unspecified country in Asia. He met up with the woman, whom he had met months earlier, and eventually traveled to Georgia, where he got a job and an apartment, LaSpisa said.

LaSpisa said Borgwardt paid $30,000 in financial restitution to local law enforcement and agreed to submit a DNA sample and pay court costs. While she said this “cannot begin to fix the damage he has done, it tells our community that we will hold individuals accountable, and it may also act as a future deterrent to future destructive plans such as this.”

Jonathan Edwards contributed to this report.
item.author: Annabelle Timsit

item.title: 美媒披露美方重建加沙计划：欲控制该地区至少10年；多地公布今年七夕结婚登记数据
item.description:
第一财经每日早间精选热点新闻，点击「听新闻」，一键收听。

【今日推荐】

俄罗斯总统普京乘机抵达天津 出席2025年上合组织峰会

31日上午，俄罗斯总统普京乘机抵达天津，出席2025年上合组织峰会。这也是普京总统继去年5月来华进行国事访问后，再一次开启中国之行。结束在天津的行程后，普京总统还将前往北京，出席中国人民抗日战争暨世界反法西斯战争胜利80周年纪念活动。俄方透露，跟随普京总统一同来华的，还有一个“规模庞大、意义重大”的代表团，其中包括三位副总理、十多位部长以及各大企业代表。

多地公布今年七夕结婚登记数据，上海创近十年来七夕结婚登记量新高

8月29日正逢中国传统“七夕”节，也是婚姻登记“全国通办”后首个七夕节。多地迎来结婚登记小高峰。截至29日17时30分，广东全省共办理结婚登记10558对，其中“全国通办”2452对。8月29日，上海全市共有2310对新人办理结婚登记，创近十年来七夕节当天结婚登记量新高。

美媒披露美方重建加沙计划：欲控制该地区至少10年

当地时间8月31日，美媒披露，特朗普政府内部正在考虑一项由美方主导的加沙地带重建计划。在此计划中，美方将控制加沙地带至少10年，并希望将其重建为“旅游胜地和制造业中心”。

【观国内】

制造业PMI回升至49.4%，“反内卷”政策效果显现

随着高温多雨影响减弱以及稳经济稳就业政策举措落地见效，经济景气水平有所回升。国家统计局8月31日发布的8月份制造业采购经理指数（PMI）为49.4%，比上月上升0.1个百分点，制造业景气水平有所改善。非制造业商务活动指数为50.3%，比上月上升0.2个百分点，非制造业继续保持扩张。

1—7月职工医保个人账户共济2.31亿人次 共济金额304.57亿元

据国家医保局消息，目前，职工医保个人账户共济可以通过即时调用被绑定人个人账户、医保钱包转账等方式实现。2025年1—7月职工医保个人账户共济人次2.31亿，金额304.57亿元。

水利部和中国气象局联合发布黄色山洪灾害气象预警

水利部和中国气象局8月31日18时联合发布黄色山洪灾害气象预警：预计，8月31日20时至9月1日20时，吉林东部、黑龙江东南部、湖北东北部、重庆东南部、西藏西北部、新疆中部和东北部等地部分地区可能发生山洪灾害（蓝色预警），其中，吉林东部、黑龙江东南部、西藏西北部等地部分地区发生山洪灾害可能性较大（黄色预警）。其他地区也可能因局地短历时强降水引发山洪灾害，请各地注意做好实时监测、防汛预警和转移避险等防范工作。

中国汽车流通协会：8月中国汽车经销商库存预警指数为57.0%

8月31日，中国汽车流通协会发布数据显示，2025年8月中国汽车经销商库存预警指数为57.0%，同比上升0.8个百分点，环比下降0.2个百分点。库存预警指数位于荣枯线之上，汽车流通行业景气度有所下降。

2025年中国电影总票房突破400亿元

网络平台数据显示，2025年度中国电影总票房（含海外）突破400亿元。其中，国内市场总票房392.3亿元，观影人次超9.09亿，均超去年同期。今年以来，在《哪吒之魔童闹海》《南京照相馆》等影片带动下，中国电影海外市场票房折合人民币已超7.7亿元，创下多年新高。

挂科也有资格保研，多所高校明确不再“一票否决”

过去，高校保研普遍实行“一票否决”，即有过挂科的学生直接被排除在推免之外。如今南京农业大学、西安交通大学、上海交通大学等多所高校对这一刚性要求作出调整。当然，挂科不再“一刀切”的政策，绝不意味着降低推免的准入门槛，能够保研的学生，整体的综合排名必须排在前列，成绩排名的硬指标还是关键。

广东：8月24日至30日新增报告225例基孔肯雅热本地个案

广东省疾控局发布8月24日至30日广东省基孔肯雅热监测信息：2025年8月24日0时至8月30日24时，全省新增报告225例基孔肯雅热本地个案，未报告重症和死亡个案。病例分布在佛山119例，广州49例，深圳16例，湛江14例，潮州5例，中山4例，珠海、汕头各3例，江门、清远、东莞各2例，韶关、肇庆、惠州、梅州、汕尾、云浮各1例。

【览海外】

联合国秘书长强烈谴责胡塞武装拘押联合国人员

当地时间8月31日，联合国秘书长古特雷斯通过发言人办公室发表声明，强烈谴责胡塞武装当日在其控制地区任意拘押至少11名联合国工作人员的行为。

特朗普要向芝加哥派兵 市长拒绝配合

美国第三大城市芝加哥的市长8月30日签署一份行政令，对特朗普政府向该市部署大批联邦执法人员和国民警卫队的计划表示“拒绝配合”。芝加哥市长、民主党人布兰登·约翰逊说，该行政令表明，芝加哥市警察局不会配合联邦国民警卫队及其他执法人员在该市的行动，包括巡逻、交通拦停和设检查站等。他还指示该市警察必须身穿正式警服、不戴任何遮面用具，以便表明身份、区别于联邦所派部队，避免民众误认。

美媒：与莫迪关系降温，特朗普或取消秋季访印行程

美媒8月31日报道，美国总统特朗普近期曾多次尝试与印度总理莫迪通话，却屡遭冷落。美媒称，由于与莫迪关系降温，特朗普将可能取消秋季的印度之行及出席“四方安全对话”的计划。

黎议长拒绝支持美方提出的解除真主党武装计划

当地时间8月31日，黎巴嫩议长贝里发表讲话，拒绝支持美方提出的黎真主党解除武装计划。贝里在讲话中说，黎方愿意就真主党武器的去向进行讨论，但相关讨论必须在“平静和一致同意”的对话框架下进行，而不是在外国势力的威胁下。

韩国医生“辞职潮”风波持续18个月后终平息

韩国实习和住院医生因反对医学院扩招计划而引发的“辞职潮”风波持续18个月后终于平息，大部分涉事医生将于9月1日返岗，韩国医疗系统人手紧缺的状况有望得以缓解。韩国多家媒体援引业内消息人士的话报道，各大医院已完成今年下半年实习和住院医生的招聘工作，返岗和新聘医生的具体数量将由保健福祉部在数日内公布。按媒体说法，此前离岗的大部分医生均已同意返回。

泰国总理争夺战开打，他信家族能否续写传奇

佩通坦“通话门”案尘埃落定后，争夺下一任泰国总理“宝座”的竞争已然开始。8月29日，泰国宪法法院裁决佩通坦违反宪法，解除其总理职务。目前符合总理候选人资格的共有五人，但竞争主要在佩通坦所在的为泰党推选的候选人猜格森，与自豪泰党党首阿努廷之间展开。

巴基斯坦与亚美尼亚建交

当地时间8月31日，巴基斯坦外交部发表声明称，巴基斯坦副总理兼外长达尔与亚美尼亚外长米尔佐扬正式互换联合公报，两国由此建立外交关系。巴基斯坦外交部表示，两国外长重申了对《联合国宪章》原则和宗旨的承诺，并探讨了在经济、教育、文化和旅游等领域合作的可能性。

【大公司】

李斌称ES8正在紧急加产能，记者实探蔚来门店

8月29日下午，蔚来创始人、董事长、CEO李斌表示，全新ES8预定情况不错，原先觉得能达到L90一样的水平就不错，现在来看情况还要更好一些。全新ES8预售价在比二代价格下探十来万后，市场到底买不买单？第一财经记者周末实探位于上海的蔚来门店。

美团和京东拼抢“线下折扣店”，刘强东现身“助阵”

8月30日，京东折扣超市在公司创始人刘强东的老家宿迁四店齐开。京东表示，该折扣超市背靠京东供应链体系，多款特色商品产地直采、源头直发，消除中间环节溢价。而在前一天8月29日，刘强东也现身宿迁，为折扣超市的开业预热。除了京东，美团和盒马近期在线下折扣零售赛道也更新了动作。

【掘金圈】

9月财经日历请查收！

本周逾188亿元市值限售股解禁

本周（9月1日至5日）共有29家公司限售股陆续解禁，合计解禁20.13亿股，按8月29日收盘价计算，解禁总市值为188.77亿元，均较上周大幅减少。个股来看，福田汽车、富特科技、益诺思、奥浦迈、莱茵生物、五芳斋、速达股份等解禁市值较大，均超过10亿元。

本周将有1只新股发行

本周将有1只新股发行。艾芬达将在9月1日发行，本次发行价格为27.69元/股，申购代码为301575。

【一财精选】

上海团险版商保目录呼之欲出，新型团险定价“兼顾惠民属性”

第一财经独家了解到，目前，在上海医保及金融监管等多部门指导下，上海头部商业健康险公司正在联合研发新型团险产品，并以此为样板制定新型团险示范性条款。目前，数款创新产品已进入最后攻坚阶段，预计与示范性条款一起，在今年下半年同步面市。据多名深度参与到相关工作的保司人士透露，新型团险产品会引入团险版商保药品目录，聚焦医保外保障责任，探索共保体等风险共担机制，并有望在企业员工家属保障责任拓宽、个人医疗费用“封顶”等方面进行试点探索。

被裁定大部分关税“非法”！特朗普政府打到最高法，前景如何？输了要赔光？

8月30日清晨，不少外贸微信群一下活跃起来，被一则“美国上诉法院裁定特朗普政府实施大部分全球关税非法”的新闻瞬间刷屏。一位物流业资深人士对第一财经记者表示，真希望判决马上生效，这样还能少交几天关税，但也深知该案件大概率要继续进入美国最高法院的审理程序，耗时漫长。

item.title: 证监会重磅发声；中芯国际拟收购控股子公司剩余股权
item.description:
机构认为，成长占优依然是市场主要方向，可关注科技成长内部的行情扩散机会。

【财经日历】

个人消费贷款财政贴息政策正式实施；

《人工智能生成合成内容标识办法》正式施行；

《电动自行车安全技术规范》正式实施；

吉林省实施境外旅客购物离境退税政策；

上证基准做市公司债指数编制方案修订正式实施；

第二十三届中国国际装备制造业博览会于9月1日至4日在沈阳举办；

美股因劳工节假期休市。

当地时间上周五，美股全线下挫，截至收盘，道指跌0.20%，纳指跌1.15%，标普500指数跌0.64%。

明星科技股表现低迷，英伟达跌3.3%，苹果跌0.2%，微软跌0.6%，亚马逊跌1.1%，特斯拉跌3.5%，谷歌逆势上涨0.6%。

纳斯达克中国金龙指数收涨1.5%，阿里巴巴涨12.9%，创2023年3月以来最大涨幅，公司云计算业务收入增长强劲，百度涨4.7%，京东涨2.2%，网易、拼多多则跌超1%。

个股方面，费城半导体指数下跌3.2%，创4月份以来最大跌幅。英伟达股价下跌3.3%，公司最新财报没有达到投资者的高预期，但显示与人工智能基础设施相关的支出仍然强劲。迈威尔科技重挫19%，公司三季度业绩指引令投资者失望。

戴尔跌近9%，此前这家个人电脑制造商预测本季度利润低于预期。

避险情绪推高金价，纽约商品交易所11月交割的COMEX黄金期货涨1.17%，报3512.40美元/盎司。

经济数据方面，美联储首选的通胀指标——个人消费支出（PCE）价格指数在7月份同比上涨2.6%，核心PCE价格指数同比增长加快至2.9%。

►►国常会：
-研究在全国部分地区实施要素市场化配置综合改革试点工作；
-部署开展县域普通高中振兴行动；
-审议通过《医疗卫生强基工程实施方案》；

►►近日证监会党委书记、主席吴清在北京召开专题座谈会，与部分高校和行业机构专家学者、中国资本市场学会会员深入交流，充分听取意见建议。吴清强调，科学制定和接续实施五年规划，是我们党治国理政一条重要经验，也是中国特色社会主义一个重要政治优势。“十五五”时期是基本实现社会主义现代化夯实基础、全面发力的关键时期，也是资本市场迈向高质量发展的关键阶段。近年来，资本市场改革开放持续深化，防风险、强监管和高质量发展扎实推进，为“十四五”收官、“十五五”开局奠定了良好基础。下一步，证监会将深入贯彻党中央、国务院决策部署，高质量谋划好资本市场贯彻实施“十五五”规划相关工作。持续巩固资本市场回稳向好势头，以深化投融资综合改革为牵引，加快推进新一轮资本市场改革开放，不断增强市场的吸引力和包容性，积极倡导长期投资、价值投资、理性投资理念。专家学者、学会会员作为资本市场领域的重要研究力量，希望大家充分发挥专业优势，用好中国资本市场学会平台，加强资本市场重大战略性前沿性基础性问题研究。

►►国家统计局发布数据，8月份，制造业采购经理指数（PMI）为49.4%，比上月上升0.1个百分点，制造业景气水平有所改善。从企业规模看，大型企业PMI为50.8%，比上月上升0.5个百分点，高于临界点；中型企业PMI为48.9%，比上月下降0.6个百分点，低于临界点；小型企业PMI为46.6%，比上月上升0.2个百分点，低于临界点。从分类指数看，在构成制造业PMI的5个分类指数中，生产指数和供应商配送时间指数均高于临界点，新订单指数、原材料库存指数和从业人员指数低于临界点。

►►据自然资源部消息，《永久基本农田保护红线管理办法》公布，自2025年10月1日起施行。其中提到，永久基本农田划定后，任何单位和个人不得擅自调整、占用或者改变用途。禁止在生态保护红线、城镇开发边界调整过程中，擅自调整永久基本农田保护红线。城镇开发边界范围内的永久基本农田，原则上应当予以保留。对零星破碎、不便耕种，确需进行集中连片整治的，应当优先在城镇开发边界范围内补划，且总面积不减少；确需调出城镇开发边界范围的，应当确保城镇开发边界规模不扩大。

►►据“微信珊瑚安全”公众号消息，根据《人工智能生成合成内容标识办法》要求，平台应对AI生成合成内容添加显式标识和隐式标识。为保障用户信息获取的透明度与可信度，平台进一步优化内容识别能力。用户通过平台获取的AI生成合成内容，可能带有显式标识或隐式标识。平台也会对可能是AI生成合成的内容进行相应提示，以便用户清晰辨识。为避免发布的内容在传播过程中引起混淆或误认，用户发布的内容为AI生成合成的，发布时需主动进行声明。

►►网络平台数据显示，2025年度中国电影总票房（含海外）突破400亿元。其中，国内市场总票房392.3亿元，观影人次超9.09亿，均超去年同期。今年以来，在《哪吒之魔童闹海》《南京照相馆》等影片带动下，中国电影海外市场票房折合人民币已超7.7亿元，创下多年新高。

华虹公司：拟购买华力微97.4988%股权 股票复牌

华虹公司公告，公司拟以发行股份及支付现金的方式向上海华虹（集团）有限公司、上海集成电路产业投资基金股份有限公司、国家集成电路产业投资基金二期股份有限公司、上海国投先导集成电路私募投资基金合伙企业（有限合伙）等4名上海华力微电子有限公司股东购买其持有的华力微97.4988%股权并募集配套资金。公司股票将于2025年9月1日开市起复牌。本次交易事项尚需公司股东大会审议，并经有权监管机构批准、审核和注册后方可正式实施，尚存在较大不确定性。

中芯国际：筹划发行A股购买控股子公司中芯北方少数股权 股票停牌

中芯国际公告，公司正在筹划以发行人民币普通股（A股）的方式购买公司控股子公司中芯北方集成电路制造（北京）有限公司的少数股权，公司股票自2025年9月1日开市起开始停牌，预计停牌时间不超过10个交易日。本次交易预计不构成重大资产重组，不构成重组上市，但构成关联（连）交易。公司已与中芯北方少数股东的主要股东方签署《资产购买意向协议》，但具体交易方案仍在商讨论证中，尚存在不确定性。

中国重工：公司股票将于9月5日终止上市

中国重工公告，公司收到上交所决定对公司A股股票予以终止上市。公司A股股票终止上市暨摘牌日为2025年9月5日，不进入退市整理期交易。公司A股股票终止上市后，将按照1:0.1339的比例转换为中国船舶的A股股票。公司A股股东的股票账户中不再显示公司A股股票，直至转换完成。

贵州茅台：控股股东拟增持30亿-33亿元公司股票

贵州茅台公告，公司控股股东中国贵州茅台酒厂（集团）有限责任公司计划自本次增持公告发布之日起6个月内，通过集中竞价交易方式增持公司股票，拟增持金额不低于人民币30亿元（含）且不高于人民币33亿元（含）。增持主要基于对公司长期价值的认可和未来发展的信心，以进一步支持公司高质量可持续发展。

赛力斯：上半年净利润29.41亿元，同比增长81.03%

赛力斯公告，2025年上半年营业收入624.02亿元，同比下降4.06%；归属于上市公司股东的净利润29.41亿元，同比增长81.03%。
